summary:
We developed a real-time tactical Heads-Up Display (HUD) and surface navigation app tailored for human Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) in Deuteronilus Mensae, a high-priority Martian region rich in buried glacial water ice that acts as a cosmic shield for preserved ancient microbial biosignatures.

Because Deuteronilus Mensae features treacherous periglacial hazards like collapsing "brain terrain" fissures, steep talus slopes, and shifting debris aprons, our HUD dynamically routes astronauts along low-exertion traverse corridors directly to shallow subsurface ice targets for core sampling.

To protect crew during time-constrained EVAs, a persistent Radiation & Oxygen Countdown Bar calculates safe remaining EVA time using live solar particle flux and metabolic exertion rates. If a Solar Particle Event (SPE) hits, the interface automatically clears non-essential overlays and projects a high-contrast extraction vector toward the nearest pressurized rover or natural terrain shield, enabling safe resource harvesting and scalable deployment for future planetary missions.

Project Details: Interplanetary Survival Guide — Martian Map (Team STARBOUND)

1. What It Does & How It Works

The Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map is an offline-capable, dual-layer 3D spatial navigation and survival co-pilot built for astronauts conducting Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) on Mars. Because radio communications between Earth and Mars suffer a 4-to-24-minute one-way light-time delay, astronauts cannot rely on Mission Control in Houston for real-time hazard avoidance. Our application solves this by operating as an autonomous, habitat-hosted navigation engine:

  • Planetary Overview (Global Layer): Renders an interactive 3D globe of Mars wrapped in orbital satellite imagery, categorizing landing sites by exploration readiness—from high-confidence surveyed zones (Jezero Crater, Gale Crater) and candidate human ice-mining sites (Arcadia Planitia) to unmapped regions requiring precursor robotic scouting.
    • Slope Gradients ($>22^\circ$): Flagged as impassable tip-over zones to account for a pressurized spacesuit’s shifted center of gravity.
    • Thermal Inertia & Albedo: Identifies loose, powdery regolith dust traps versus solid bedrock footing.
    • Sky-View Factor: Pre-computes topographic shielding along steep crater walls, cliff overhangs, and lava tube skylights to designate natural radiation shelters.
  • Zero-Latency Emergency Evacuation Mode: Continuously monitors local spacesuit and habitat telemetry (modeled on real Perseverance MEDA weather logs and Curiosity RAD radiation datasets). If a threshold is breached—such as a Solar Particle Event (SPE) radiation spike ($>2.0\text{ mSv/hr}$), a sudden barometric pressure drop ($\Delta P$) signaling an approaching dust devil, or high atmospheric optical depth ($\tau > 1.5$) during a dust storm—the system immediately aborts the science traverse, calculates the fastest safe path to the nearest shielded shelter ("Safe Haven"), and displays a countdown against acute exposure limits.
  • ARES Edge-AI Co-Pilot: An onboard, locally hosted LLM assistant that automatically ingests the astronaut’s live coordinates, terrain metrics, and telemetry snapshot to answer tactical field questions or trigger route recalculations with zero Earth communication lag.

2. Key Benefits

  • Eliminates Earth-Mars Latency Risk: Enables instant life-saving routing decisions locally on the habitat server or suit computer without waiting up to 48 minutes for a round-trip signal from Earth.
  • Balances Science Productivity with Crew Safety: Rather than treating Mars purely as an obstacle course, the pathfinder optimizes routes that connect priority astrobiology and In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) sampling sites while respecting suit oxygen and slope limits.
  • Future-Proof & Extensible: Includes a custom mission data ingestion module allowing future mission planners to upload new HiRISE terrain grids or sensor logs as new regions of Mars are mapped.

3. Intended Impact

The project bridges the operational gap between NASA’s existing regional orbital viewers (which are designed for broad planetary science) and the hyperlocalized, real-time tactical HUD required by human explorers on the surface. By integrating orbital hazard mapping, spacesuit mobility constraints, and edge-AI decision support into a unified interface, the tool provides a scalable blueprint for safe human surface operations on Mars—and can be adapted for lunar South Pole Artemis EVAs where extreme lighting shadows and radiation hazards pose similar challenges.

4. Tools, Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • 3D Geospatial & Mapping Engine: CesiumJS, Cesium ion (Cesium Mars 3D Tileset combining MOLA/Mars Express terrain with Viking global mosaics and high-res Jezero/Gale Crater imagery), and NASA JPL Mars Trek WMTS tile services.
  • Scientific Datasets: USGS / HiRISE Digital Terrain Models (DTMs) for slope and sky-view factor math; Mars Odyssey THEMIS thermal inertia layers; MRO CRISM mineral overlays; NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) Perseverance MEDA (weather/dust opacity) and Curiosity RAD (surface radiation) telemetry logs.
  • Frontend & Spatial Logic: React, TypeScript/JavaScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and geospatial pathfinding algorithms (A* / Dijkstra cost-weighted routing).
  • Edge AI & Development Environment: Local LLM inference via Ollama (gemma-4-31b-it), developed and visually verified using Google Antigravity and its browser testing agent.

5. Creativity & Innovation

  • Turning Orbital Physics into Walking Rules: Instead of displaying raw scientific heatmaps that require a planetary geologist to interpret, we translated abstract orbital measurements—like Thermal Inertia and Sky-View Factor—into intuitive survival rules ("Hidden Soft Dust Trap" and "Natural Radiation Shelter").
  • Telemetry-Injected Edge AI: Rather than building a disconnected chatbot, the onboard AI silently reads the astronaut’s exact telemetry state (slope, thermal_inertia, radiation_msv_hr, dust_tau) on every query, turning raw sensor anomalies into actionable field guidance.
  • Dual-Mode Mission Architecture: Seamlessly shifts the entire UI from a calm, exploratory Science Traverse Planner into a high-contrast, time-critical Emergency Shelter Router the instant an environmental threshold is crossed.

6. Factors Our Team Considered

  • Human Biomechanics in Spacesuits: Pressurized EVA suits restrict visibility, raise the astronaut's center of gravity, and increase metabolic oxygen burn on inclines, requiring strict slope-angle penalties rather than standard walking distances.
  • Communication & Power Constraints: Designed the system to run completely offline on local habitat hardware so a loss of Earth downlink or cloud connectivity never degrades astronaut navigation.
  • Data Gaps & Planetary Protection: Explicitly distinguished well-mapped landing zones from unmapped terrain requiring precursor scouting, while marking potential subsurface water-ice margins as high-priority ISRU/Planetary Protection zones.
  • Usability Under Stress: Minimized cognitive load during emergencies by replacing dense data tables with color-coded hazard zones, clear shelter vectors, and time-to-threshold countdowns.
